11.0.s.en: 1. Let us not grow weary in practical love:

11.0.0.en: 1 Cast your bread upon the waters, for you shall find it after many days. 2 Give a portion to seven, and also to eight, for you do not know what evil shall be upon the earth. 3 If the clouds are full of rain, they empty it upon the earth; and if the tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it shall be. 4 He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the clouds will not reap. 5 As you do not know what is the way of the wind, nor how the bones grow in the womb of her who is with child, even so you do not know the works of God who makes all. 6 In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not withhold your hand, for you do not know which will prosper, whether this or that, or whether both of them will be alike good.

11.0.1.en: The wise man offers us examples to reveal the necessity of constant striving in the work of love:

11.0.2.en: a. “Cast your bread upon the waters, for you shall find it after many days” [1].

11.0.3.en: This proverb points to generosity in giving. If the waters signify the many nations (Rev 16:5), then it is fitting for a person to cast, not only good words, but his bread, that is, from his own needs, to many, without expecting a quick recompense, but rather after many days. The work may seem outwardly to be without wisdom, since it is casting bread upon the face of the waters, so that many share your needs; but it floats and returns to you at the proper time.

11.0.4.en: Perhaps the casting of bread here indicates that almsgiving, or practical love, is like a ship sailing on the face of the waters to carry what we have safely to the heavenly harbor.

11.0.5.en: * It is believed that it is far better to be generous even to the unworthy for the sake of the worthy (that is, lest we wrong a person who deserves to receive, while we think him undeserving). It seems that this is our duty, to cast our bread upon the face of the waters, for it will not be swept far away or lost before the eyes of the just Examiner, but will reach Him, and He will gather it for us as a portion that we shall receive in due time, even if we doubt that this will happen.

11.0.6.en: St. Gregory the Wonderworker It also points to the life of sincere repentance, in which God brings us into “rivers of waters in a straight way” (Jer 31:9). When the tears of repentance become our daily bread, our souls walk upon the face of the water in safety... and it carries us from the valley of tears to the joyful heavenly life.

11.0.7.en: * Cast your bread upon the face of the waters, and you will find the bread of heaven where the waters of grace are... for out of the belly flow rivers of living water (Jn 7:38)... and you will feed on mystical food.

11.0.8.en: Where there are the waters of tears and the rest of repentance, you feed on the living bread; for it is written: “They shall come with weeping, and with supplications will I lead them” (Jer 31:9).

11.0.9.en: Blessed are those whose tears are their bread, for they will be made worthy of joy... “Blessed are ye that weep” (Lk 6:21).

11.0.10.en: St. Ambrose This proverb also points to the life of daring in striving: a person casts his bread, which he needs, upon the face of the waters, assured that God will return it to him at the proper time, as the Apostle says: “For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love” (Heb 6:10).

11.1.0.en: b. “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight, for you do not know what evil shall be upon the earth” [2].

11.1.1.en: Some see that this proverb points to continual giving: if you meet seven poor people, give to them generously, and if eight come to you after them, do not excuse yourself that you have already done good, but continue giving, because you do not know what will befall you... They are in need now; perhaps you will be in need tomorrow. Let us do good like God, who gives generously and does not reproach.

11.1.2.en: The number 7 points to the present life, and the number 8 points to the other life, after death. Let us strive all the days of our sojourn, that we may obtain temporal blessings and heavenly ones; or let us strive with love in what concerns temporal matters and also in what concerns spiritual matters, that is, let us give practical love by generosity in giving, by witnessing for the salvation of our brethren, and by caring for their eternity... By this you are kept from evil.

11.1.3.en: St. Basil the Great speaks to us about the necessity of being committed to seriousness in the daily work that concerns our temporal life, and of being faithful in what concerns our spiritual striving, saying:

11.1.4.en: [The prohibition of excessive care for the needs of our body does not at all negate care and work. For it remains for us “to labour for ourselves, not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life” (Jn 6:27), not only for our bodily need, but also to help our neighbor (Eph 4:28)...].

11.1.5.en: Others see that the number 7 points to the Old Testament, with its promises of temporal blessings, and the number 8 points to the New Testament, with its promises of blessings of the world to come... Let us then be faithful in carrying out the commandment of love and in striving in it, so that we may fulfill the commandment of both Testaments and enjoy the word of God, which upholds us against every evil.

11.1.6.en: * It was said in Ecclesiastes with reference to the two Testaments: “Give a portion of what you have to seven, and even to eight.”

11.1.7.en: St. Augustine * It was rightly said: “Give a portion of what you have to seven, and to eight also,” for those who have fed on the Law and been crowned with grace receive a portion by grace through either number.

11.1.8.en: St. Ambrose * The ark had its chambers, and the Church has many mansions (the plural of “station”), and eight souls were saved in Noah's ark; and Ecclesiastes counsels us: “Give a portion of what you have to seven, and even to eight,” that is, believe in both Testaments.

11.1.9.en: St. Jerome * The reverence given to the number 7 makes us also revere the day of Pentecost (the fiftieth), because seven multiplied by seven gives the number 50 less one day, which we borrow from the age to come, that is, the eighth or the first, or rather the day that does not pass away; for the sabbath rest of our souls now ceases there, where a portion is given to seven, and even to eight.

11.2.0.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus c. “If the clouds are full of rain, they empty it upon the earth” [3].

11.2.1.en: The believer is like the cloud that overflows with love, like the rain that turns the wildernesses into fruitful gardens.

11.2.2.en: * Give generously; give a portion of what you have to many, even to one who does not know what the coming day holds in store for him. For the clouds do not hold back the abundance of rain within them, but pour out what is in them upon the face of the earth; and the tree does not remain in its place forever, even if people protect it, for the wind may bring it down at some time.

11.2.3.en: St. Gregory the Wonderworker d. “And if the tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it shall be” [3].

11.2.4.en: In the Bible the north wind signifies spiritual coldness, and the south wind, coming from the tropical regions, signifies spiritual warmth. The truly spiritual person is like a fruitful tree wherever he is found, whether in the south or in the north, that is, in circumstances that inflame the heart spiritually or among those who are spiritually cold; under all circumstances he does not cease striving for the edification of all who are around him. Wherever he settles, he feels that God has brought him there to offer good, regardless of the conditions and characteristics of those around him.

11.3.0.en: e. “He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the clouds will not reap” [4].

11.3.1.en: The fearful person stays in his place without working; he fears the winds and so does not sow, and fears the rains and so does not reap, as though the writer urges us to work without hesitation and without fear of the existence of obstacles and difficulties.

11.3.2.en: In Egypt the month of Amshir, which is the month of winds and storms, is considered the month for planting trees (transplanting the seedling and planting it)...

11.3.3.en: Many cloak themselves with wisdom when they are afraid to practice good works and hold back from them. Therefore St. Isaac the Syrian says: [Do not let an abundance of wisdom become a stumbling block to your soul and a snare in your path, but let steadfast trust in God make for you the beginning of the way that is filled with blood (the way of spiritual struggle against sin), lest you be found continually in want and stripped of the knowledge of God, for the fearful man who watches the wind never sows].

11.4.0.en: f. “As you do not know what is the way of the wind, nor how the bones grow in the womb of her who is with child, so we do not know the works of God who makes all” [5].

11.4.1.en: Let us practice the work of love continually without fear, trusting in God, who works in nature on our behalf and who works in our lives; for it is He who set the laws of the winds with wondrous precision, and it is He who creates the bones of a person while he is in his mother's womb. We do not know precisely the movement of the wind or how the bones are created, but we enjoy the wondrous works of God, which cannot be comprehended.

11.4.2.en: In other words, the wise man asks us to practice practical love with our brethren without human calculations, trusting in His promises to us that He repays us our love for our brethren with His surpassing love, in ways that exceed our plans and our understanding.

11.4.3.en: g. Let us strive in the way of practical love all the days of our life:

11.5.0.en: “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not withhold your hand, for you do not know which will prosper, whether this or that, or whether both of them will be alike good” [7].

11.5.1.en: Sow the work of love in the time of joy (the morning) and also in the midst of sufferings (the evening), for you may win a soul by revealing your sincere love for it, either in the midst of its joy or of its troubles, or in both.

11.5.2.en: Strive in works of love in the morning of your life, that is, from your childhood, boyhood and youth, and also in the evening, which is old age... Whenever the opportunity is offered you, work, and do not slacken your hand, pleading that you are still young, lest you say in your old age that the time for work has been lost.

11.5.3.en: Let us rise early, offering the firstfruits of our time to the work of the Lord, and let us remain working until the end of our time, for if we live, we live unto the Lord, and if we die, we die unto the Lord; whether we live or die, we are the Lord's.

11.5.4.en: If our Christ, because of His love for us, was crucified, suffered and died to raise us with Him, it is fitting for us also to strive with love with Him and in Him, to be crucified with Him that we may rise with Him.

11.5.5.en: * If the Lord ascended the Cross on Friday, rested on Saturday, and rose from the dead on Sunday, so the mind, unless it ascends the Cross and tastes the vinegar and the myrrh, and then enters into rest from pains, is not worthy of the resurrection from its fall.

11.5.6.en: * As ploughed ground brings forth seed, so youth, because of the heat of its sharp movements, loves constant work, lest instead of good seed it bring forth thorns and thistles... (idleness is very bad)...

11.5.7.en: St. John Saba * We must die to sin and be crucified with Christ, placing all our love in Him. This is hard. But what is easy in the order of goodness? Victories are not gained by much sleep, nor are the crowns of triumph reaped in pleasures and the sound of trumpets... He who strives wins, and by labors we obtain glory.

11.6.s.en: 2. A call to work for the young:

11.6.0.en: 7 Truly the light is sweet, and a good thing it is for the eyes to behold the sun. 8 For if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all, and let him remember the days of darkness, for they shall be many. All that comes is vanity. 9 Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth, and walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes; but know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment. 10 Therefore remove sorrow from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh, for childhood and youth are vanity.

11.6.1.en: We ought not only to strive in the spirit of love, but also to start early in our striving, beginning our life with God in our youth; and the Preacher has revealed the motives for fellowship with God at an early age:

11.7.s.en: a. “The light is sweet, and it is good for the eyes to behold the sun” [7].

11.7.0.en: It is not a call to hard labor involving deprivation, but a call to enjoy the heavenly light, which gives illumination to the eyes, so that our inner man looks upon the splendor of God's glory and perceives His joyful heavens... we see Him as the Sun of Righteousness.

11.7.1.en: * The city of the person pure in soul is in his depths, and the sun that shines in it is the light of the Holy Spirit.

11.7.2.en: * Flee from the lusts of the world so that the light flowing from the Father may meet you, and commend you to His angels who serve His mysteries, that they may free you from your bonds, and you may walk following in His steps to the (bosom of) the Father.

11.7.3.en: * Faith in Christ is a life-giving and rational light.

11.7.4.en: St. Isaac the Syrian * Blessed is he who is worthy to enter there (the land of the spiritual ones), where the soul beholds the face of its Lord, tastes the sweetness of its God and rejoices, breathes in His pure fragrance, is enclosed in the depth of His greatness, is illumined by the ray of His beauty, and clings to Him, and does not want to leave from there.

11.7.5.en: This is the Rapture which our fathers call the vision of the glory of God. This is the pledge of the new world.

11.7.6.en: * You, my Lord, are the sun of the prudent, and from You they are illumined without interruption.

11.7.7.en: * Blessed is he who always gazes upon You within himself, for his heart is lit up to see hidden things.

11.7.8.en: * We cannot behold the sun without clear air and eyes free from disease; so we cannot behold the Sun of Righteousness while He is in the heaven of the heart without faith, love and patience.

11.7.9.en: St. John Saba The Lord Christ is the light of the world; He enlightens the eyes. He enlightens the right eye, so that it looks at eternal and spiritual things through Him, and He enlightens the left, so that it looks at temporal things also through Him, so that the believer sees the Lord Christ transfigured in his life and in his eternal and temporal aspirations, or in his worship and his daily work... He sees everything as sanctified in Him.

11.8.0.en: “For if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all...

11.8.1.en: Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth...” [8-9].

11.8.2.en: The living young person hates gloom, and God, in His love for man, wants for him a life of inner joy as food on which the soul feeds and its youth is renewed. It rejoices in the depths and translates its joy through practical conduct, in what the heart sees (the inner life) and what the eyes behold (the outward conduct).

11.8.3.en: * Two beautiful virtues are love and joy.

11.8.4.en: Love kills and puts to death the corrupt movements of the mind (such as anger, envy, etc.)...

11.8.5.en: And joy awakens and gives life to the luminous movements.

11.8.6.en: Body and soul both delight in the Lord through love and joy.

11.8.7.en: St. John Saba St. Anthony sees that joy is the food of the soul, on which it feeds in order to grow, and St. Basil the Great sees that gloom, or deprivation of joy, is the destruction of the inner man, for he says: [Gloom is drunkenness, for it extinguishes the light of the mind and blots out the light in it].

11.8.8.en: The wise man asks us to rejoice all the days of our life [8]... Does no sorrow then pass over us? In Christ Jesus we enjoy the joy of the Spirit (Gal 5:22), which the world cannot take away from our depths.

11.8.9.en: What increases our joy is that we remember the many days of darkness [8]; we remember how our Christ lifted us up to the light and removed from us the weight of our sins... we remember our weakness and are contrite, and we remember His work of salvation and our souls exult.

11.9.0.en: Let us also rejoice because, if we enter into sufferings, they grant us glories in the Lord, for he says: “for all these things God will bring you into judgment” [9].

11.10.s.en: c. The Preacher affirms the link between gloom and evil:

11.10.0.en: Let us leave evil, to flee from gloom; let us be joined to the righteousness of Christ, to enjoy the joy of His Holy Spirit, for he says: “Therefore remove sorrow from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh” [10].

11.10.1.en: * The joy that is in God is stronger than this present time; whoever finds it not only does not care for (evil) lusts but will not even think of his own life, nor of anything else, if he has truly been counted worthy of that joy.

11.10.2.en: St. Isaac the Syrian * Put away grief from your body and gloom from your thoughts, apart from what your sin causes, for it puts you in constant grief.
